been, in many ways, a celebrated

We are exulting our victories, are we
not? Although the Fraternity continues to
struggle into the 20th century, it has not
fallen victim to the so-called "modern
age." The social turmoil of the Sixties
decade, the selfishly introverted "me"
generation of the Seventies, and the
feminist reaction have afl taken their tolls
on the whole fraternity system. Psi Up

ly and has not only survived but has
grown larger and is touching the hearts of
more students today than ever before.
We do, indeed, have cause for celebra

the opportunity to take part in and to
experience at first hand the commemora
tion of the Fraternity's birth by partici
pating in one of the twenty or so sched
uled Sesquicentennial Celebration din
ners to be held in cities across the United
States and Canada in the coming months.
If the Convention serves as a precur
sor, then the Sesquicentennial Celebra
tion festivities shall prove to be splendid.
The bi-weekly planning sessions for the
Convention began in early April at the
Theta Chapter House. The Theta alumni
and undergraduates, along with mem
bers ofthe Fraternity's professional staff,
quickly reahzed that this would not be
just another Convention. An appropriate
quotation taken from the writings of

ma '39, Executive Vice President:
"We are not here to play, to dream, to
drift �
We have hard work to do and loads to
lift.
Shun not the struggle �
face it �

most important legislation passed by the
140th Convention included the foflowing:
(1) Adoption of the report of the Task
Force on Hazing (which was chaired by
Bfll Robie, Epsilon Omega '66, and
Sean Mahoney, Omega '84), which

prehensive educational process, a Con
stitutional change which defines hazing
in more specific terms and enumer
ates the elements of a constructive
pledge education program, and a
mechanism for handling hazing infrac
tions.
(2) Establishment of an Undergraduate
Advisory Board for the purpose of pro
viding increased undergraduate par
ticipation in Fraternity governance.
(3) Increasing for the year 1983-84 the
Chapter tax for continuing active mem
bers from $40 to $50 per person per
year and the one-time membership fee
for new initiates from $70 to $75 per
person.
(4) Adoption of a balanced operating
budget for the year 1983-84, providing
for total receipts of $239,000 and total
expenses of $239,000.
(5) Recommendation that the Fraterni
ty's expansion efforts be directed to
ward reactivating the Sigma Chapter at

ter at the University of California at
Berkeley, and expression of further

attaining full chapter status in Psi Up
silon.
(6) Conferring ofthe Psi Upsflon Award
for Academic Distinction upon the
Zeta Chapter at Dartmouth College,
with special commendation to the Phi
Chapter at the University of Michigan.
(7) Acceptance ofthe Eta Chapter's for
mal bid to host the 141st Convention,
on the occasion ofthe Eta's Centennial
Anniversary, in 1984 at Lehigh Uni
versity.
(8) Recommendation that, for the pur

In his letter of welcome, Theta Alumni
President Tom Wefles '79 invited all par
ticipants to "relish in that special feefing,
which only we, who are tied by the bonds
of brotherhood, can really understand
. . . that special feeling of Psi Upsilon."
Although it may seem that this Conven
tion produced more legislation than Con
ventions in previous years, the opportu
nities for experiencing "that special feel
ing of Psi Upsilon" were not limited.
Throughout the four-day legislative
gathering, numerous social and com
memorative events took place.
At the opening luncheon on Thursday,
Professor C. William Huntley, retired
Dean and Provost of Union College and a
brother of Theta Delta Chi, addressed
the delegates. He spoke on the history of
the College and its special relationship
with the secret societies (Union College is
widely regarded as the "Mother of
Fraternities"). Professor Huntley sug
gested ways in which the contemporary
fratemity chapters might strive to make
Union College a better community for
young scholars. Huntley was confident
that Psi Upsilon could play a major role in
this process, as he holds Psi U in high
regard.
The first general meeting was opened
by BiU Ham, Theta '32, Convention CoChairman. Brother Ham welcomed the
delegates on behaff of the Theta Chapter,
and his remarks were followed by Presi
dent of the Executive Council Russ
McShane, Delta '32, who introduced
John S. Morris, President of Union Col
lege. President Morris extended greet
ings to the Fraternity on behalf of the
College. Alexander Turner, Theta '34,
gave a moving address ofwelcome, just as
he had done as the undergraduate Presi
dent ofthe Theta Chapter at the Centen- |
nial celebration in 1933. He entrusted his '
message to Mike Rogers, Theta '84, current undergraduate President ofthe The- I
ta, to be delivered at the Bicentennial �

Robert Field, Theta '44, officiated at a 1 1

Memorial Chapel, located just west ofthe :
Theta Chapter House. The service was ;

brothers who have passed on. Bob �

moving address, in which he capsulized
the spirit that the founding fathers
shared. The "Shrine Song" closed the ser
vice with brothers hand-linked to one
another.
On Thursday evening Dean Edward
M. King of Bradley University gave a
provocative presentation on "The Secret
Thoughts of a Ritual." Dr. King chal
lenged his audience to read, discuss,
even debate the principles and objectives
ofthe Psi Upsilon ritual (e.g., the pledge
ceremony, the formal initiation, the for
mal meeting, and other Chapter rites) in
an effort to more clearly understand the
philosophy and ideals of the Fratemity
and how they apply to life beyond the
undergraduate experience. A spon
taneous and lively round of Psi U songs
was sung prior to Dr. King's lecture, dur
ing which the official song of the Ses
quicentennial Anniversary, "Sesqui Psi
U," was rehearsed. Composed by Stan
Davies, Lambda '53, "Sesqui Psi U"
cheerfully recounts the Fraternity's first
150 years.

open house parties. While providing a

land B. Winsor, Epsilon Phi '27, pre

inal Theta Chapter minute book, which

attended the Centennial Anniversary in
November, 1933.

those who had come to Schenectady to
roll up their sleeves and set themselves to

formal attire, overlooked the gathering of

by the Reverend Robert Field following a
heartfelt rendition of the "Psi U Doxolo
gy," and toasts to the President of the

British Commonwealth were offered by
Rear Admiral Albert Stevenson, Theta

respectively.

state, and industrial dignitaries were read

testimony to the value of fraternal life."

experience of your 150th Anniversary by
declaring the week of August 22-28, 1983

greeting were received from Daniel P.
Moynihan and Alfonse M. D'Amato,
United States Senators representing New
York; New York State Governor Mario
M. Cuomo; Pierre E. Trudeau, Prime
Minister of Canada; Keith M. Caflow,

mer head coach of the St. Louis Cardi
nals.
